oneLine: To serve generative models in production you need three layers: a fast runtime on each GPU instance, infrastructure that scales and survives failures, and tooling that gives engineers the control they need.
summary:
Classic ML inference ran small models on cheap CPUs behind a thin software stack. Generative models need GPUs and far more engineering: copy the weights onto a GPU and you have a demo, with a long way to go before production.

The chapter splits the work into three layers. The **runtime** makes one model on one instance as fast and efficient as possible, using inference engines, low-level kernels and a set of techniques: batching, KV cache reuse, quantization, speculation, parallelism and disaggregation. The **infrastructure** takes over when one instance can't keep up: first autoscaling replicas, then, past a few hundred GPUs, finding capacity across regions and clouds, and finally pooling it all as one fleet. With the **tooling**, you choose how much of this engineers see, somewhere between a black-box API and raw compute.

Chapters 1 to 7 follow that map: prerequisites, models, hardware, software, techniques, modalities and production.

mechanism.title: Optimise one instance
mechanism.body: The runtime squeezes speed and efficiency out of a single model on its GPUs.

mechanism.title: Scale the fleet
mechanism.body: Infrastructure adds replicas, then capacity across regions and clouds, then one shared pool.

mechanism.title: Choose what engineers see
mechanism.body: Tooling lands between a black-box API and raw machines, trading control against productivity.

mechanism.title: Run all three
mechanism.body: Mission-critical traffic at scale needs the runtime, infrastructure and tooling working together.

callout.name: Traffic outgrows one server
callout.body: Tune one model server as far as you like and peak traffic will still outgrow it. Then you need more replicas and better placement across clusters, and no CUDA kernel gives you those.

figureRefs.lookFor: Runtime optimisations and infrastructure optimisations shown as two halves of one stack.
Speculation as an example of a runtime technique that cuts latency.
Several cloud providers' GPUs gathered into one pool of capacity.

keyCards.label: Runtime
keyCards.title: Six techniques recur all book
keyCards.body: Batching, caching, quantization, speculation, parallelism and disaggregation make one instance faster.

keyCards.label: Infrastructure
keyCards.title: Problems change with scale
keyCards.body: Autoscaling first, then capacity across clouds, then one unified pool without silos.

keyCards.label: Tooling
keyCards.title: Between black box and bare metal
keyCards.body: Engineers get enough control to trust a critical workload and enough abstraction to ship fast.

workedExample.title: Sizing replicas for a 2,400 rpm peak
workedExample.setup: An illustrative service peaks at 2,400 requests per minute. A tuned model server handles 180 requests per minute at the latency target, and the team keeps 20% headroom for spikes. Divide the peak by per-replica capacity, add the headroom, and round up to whole replicas.

conclusion.text: You can't tune one server into absorbing this peak. Running sixteen replicas and scaling them with traffic is infrastructure work, the second layer.

checkQuestion.prompt: Your single model server is as fast as it can get, but peak traffic still overwhelms it. Which of the three layers of an inference stack has to solve this next?
checkQuestion.hint: The runtime optimises one instance. Which layer deals with many instances across clusters?
checkQuestion.explanation: Infrastructure scales across replicas, clusters, regions and clouds. The runtime is tempting, but it makes one instance faster, and yours is already maxed out.
checkQuestion.sourceQuote: Scaling across clusters, regions, and clouds without creating silos while maintaining excellent uptime

reflect.prompt: A teammate says inference is just picking a fast engine like vLLM and buying GPUs. Using the three layers from Chapter 0, explain what that plan leaves out.
reflect.modelAnswer: A good engine covers part of the runtime layer. The runtime also needs kernels and techniques such as batching, KV cache reuse, quantization and speculation, and those set how much work each GPU does. Then comes infrastructure. Peak traffic will overwhelm one server, so we need autoscaling replicas, and at larger scale we need capacity across regions and cloud providers, pooled so one cluster isn't starved while another sits idle. The pool also keeps us up when a region fails. Last is tooling: engineers need enough control to run critical workloads and enough abstraction to ship fast. Buying GPUs and installing vLLM does nothing for infrastructure or tooling.
points: An engine is one piece of the runtime layer, next to kernels and techniques.
Infrastructure handles traffic beyond one instance: autoscaling, then multi-region and multi-cloud capacity.
A unified pool avoids silos and keeps the service up when a region fails.
Tooling balances control with productivity for the engineers running it.
